issues.explanation: Guilt about not doing more to stop what happened is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening accident profile unless there is clear evidence of perceived preventability or responsibility. The rest of the appraisals emphasize helplessness and unfairness rather than responsibility, so this item pulls in a different direction and is hard to explain from the provided profile.

vignette: As a social ministry worker, Rachel had always been drawn to helping others in crisis. But it was her own life-threatening accident two years ago that left her grappling with feelings of injustice and helplessness. The memory of the crash still haunted her - the screeching tires, the shattered glass, and the sense of losing control as the car careened off the road. Since then, Rachel had become increasingly wary of situations that made her feel trapped or vulnerable. When she felt physically unwell, even with something as minor as a cold, Rachel would spiral into anxiety, convinced that her body was betraying her again. She became obsessed with avoiding any situation that might put her under physical stress - no more hiking trips with friends or intense workouts at the gym. Driving had become an ordeal; she avoided getting behind the wheel whenever possible, citing fatigue or errands as excuses to stay home. The mere thought of being a passenger made her skin crawl. If she couldn't avoid driving altogether, Rachel would sit rigidly in the backseat, eyes scanning the road for potential hazards. As she navigated her daily routine, Rachel found herself perpetually on edge. Ordinary sounds - car horns, slamming doors, or even the hum of the air conditioner - made her jump. She developed a habit of scanning exits whenever she entered a room or building, always aware of the nearest escape route. Her mind was constantly racing with worst-case scenarios: what if there's a fire? What if I get trapped? The sense of unease followed her everywhere, even into her own home. Rachel couldn't shake the feeling that she had been deeply wronged by fate - that the accident was an unfair and avoidable tragedy. She replayed the moments leading up to the crash in her mind, rehashing every decision and action, wondering what she could have done differently. Her friends and family tried to reassure her, but Rachel couldn't trust their words of comfort. In her eyes, safety was just an illusion - a flimsy veil that could be ripped away at any moment. As the months passed, Rachel's fears began to reinforce each other in a vicious cycle. She avoided driving because it made her feel trapped and helpless; she felt physically unwell when she did drive because of the stress and anxiety it triggered; and she became even more hypervigilant about potential threats because her body seemed so unreliable. Her social life suffered as well - Rachel stopped attending community events or meetings, fearing that she'd be stuck in a crowded room with no clear escape. One day, while working at the ministry, Rachel received an email from a client who had been through a similar accident. The woman's story was eerily familiar - the same feelings of injustice and helplessness, the same crippling fears. For the first time, Rachel saw herself in someone else's words. It was both comforting and terrifying to realize she wasn't alone in her struggles. With a newfound sense of determination, Rachel knew it was time to seek help and confront the trauma that had been holding her back for so long. Despite her reservations, Rachel made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to break free from the cycle of fear and avoidance that had become her life. She was scared - what if she couldn't overcome these feelings? What if she was forever trapped in this prison of anxiety? But as she sat in the waiting room, Rachel steeled herself for the journey ahead, knowing it was time to take control of her own story.
